title: Broadcast Query Fan-Out — Core Method
description: A universal search begins by sending one canonical query to every connected source at the same time instead of searching sources one by one. Each source answers in its own dialect, so a thin adapter layer translates the canonical query into each source's native form before dispatch. Responses stream back asynchronously and are tagged with their origin, which keeps one slow source from blocking the rest. This is the pattern behind meta-search engines and federated library catalogs, where a single search box reaches dozens of independent collections. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — public methods from established computer-science practice.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion — Core Method
description: When several sources return their own ranked lists, reciprocal rank fusion merges them without needing comparable relevance scores. Each document earns 1/(k + rank) points from every list it appears in, with k dampening the influence of deep ranks, and the totals are sorted to form the final ranking. The method needs no training data and stays robust when sources score relevance on incompatible scales. It is a standard baseline in information retrieval for combining rankings from heterogeneous engines. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Canonical Query Model — Core Method
description: Before dispatch, the raw query is normalized into a canonical model: lowercased terms, extracted phrases, detected field filters, and a language tag. Every source adapter reads this single model instead of re-parsing the raw text, so adding a new source means writing one adapter rather than changing the core. The canonical model also records what was dropped or rewritten, which makes the whole search auditable. This separation of parsing from dispatch is what lets one interface honestly cover many different back ends. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Source Capability Registry — Core Method
description: A universal search keeps a registry describing what each source can do: which fields it indexes, which operators it supports, its typical latency, and its coverage dates. The dispatcher consults the registry to skip sources that cannot answer a query and to rewrite queries for sources with limited operators. Registries are refreshed by periodic capability probes so the system learns when a source gains a new index. Without this registry, broadcast search wastes time and budget on sources that were never going to match. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Cross-Source Deduplication — Core Method
description: The same record often lives in several archives under different identifiers, so a universal search must merge duplicates before presenting results. Content hashing — hashing a normalized form of the record text — finds exact duplicates, while shingle-based near-duplicate detection catches reworded copies. Merged records keep a provenance list of every source that held them, so nothing is lost in the merge. This step turns a pile of overlapping source hits into one clean result list. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
